Baker sees SRAM accelerators as additive to the existing GPU installed base — boosting ROI without displacing leading-edge GPUs — and notes these chips often run on older process nodes, meaning they don't compete for leading-edge fab capacity. The investment implication is that companies building SRAM-based inference accelerators represent an underappreciated opportunity, though Baker does not name specific companies, making this a thematic structural view without a directly actionable ticker at this time.

Baker draws an explicit analogy to Anthropic's revenue trajectory from $1B to $50B ARR, implying Grok could follow a similar monetization ramp, and notes that Grok 4.7 (a larger model with 1.5T+ parameters) is expected within weeks, which could further extend the quality lead. The investment implication is that investors evaluating SpaceX should materially increase the weight they assign to xAI/Grok as a revenue driver, and that the current market is undervaluing this optionality.

summary: Nvidia is likely to release a competitive open-source frontier model, funded by its chip cash flows, potentially becoming the dominant American open-source model
summary_extended: Baker argues that Nvidia is likely to release a competitive open-source frontier model in the near future, funded by its massive chip cash flows, and that this model will probably become the dominant American open-source AI model. He points to Nvidia's acquisition of Poolside — a company with strong American open-source AI talent — as deliberate preparation for this move, and notes that Jensen Huang could trivially fund a $50–100B training run given Nvidia's revenue base. The strategic logic is self-reinforcing for Nvidia: open-source models compress token margins, which drives higher token consumption, which in turn increases demand for Nvidia compute. Baker also notes that Google may pursue a parallel strategy, funding open-source training runs using TPU cash flows to entrench its own hardware ecosystem. The investment implication is that Nvidia's dominance in AI compute is further reinforced regardless of whether open or closed models win, while Google's long-term positioning in AI infrastructure may be underappreciated.

summary: SpaceX's decision to use Nvidia GPUs rather than build competing ASICs was a high-ELO strategic move that will prove wise
summary_extended: Baker argues that SpaceX's decision to use Nvidia GPUs rather than develop competing custom ASICs was a strategically superior ('high ELO') move that will be vindicated over time. His reasoning centers on the compounding advantages of plugging into Nvidia's ecosystem in a supply-constrained environment: access to Nvidia's financing programs, supply chain priority, and revenue-volume guarantees (RVGs) outweigh any marginal performance gains from proprietary silicon. Baker contrasts this favorably against hyperscalers that built their own ASICs and at times antagonized Nvidia, suggesting those relationships carry hidden costs in a world where GPU supply is the binding constraint. He offers a rule of thumb that every 1% of accelerator market share is worth approximately $100 billion in value, underscoring why competing head-on with Nvidia is irrational for most players — the better strategy is to find a niche and leverage Nvidia's ecosystem. The investment implication is straightforwardly bullish on Nvidia as the dominant, entrenched platform whose ecosystem lock-in compounds with each supply-constrained cycle.

summary: Data center buildout is re-industrializing America and is net positive for working-class Americans, with behind-the-meter power generation transforming small towns' tax revenues by 10x
summary_extended: Baker argues that the AI-driven data center buildout is the single greatest economic development for working-class Americans in recent memory, citing surging wages for electricians, plumbers, and HVAC technicians to the point where college may now be NPV-negative relative to skilled trades. He uses Loudoun County, VA — the highest per-capita income county in the US and the highest data center density county in the US — as empirical proof that data center concentration drives broad local prosperity. A key structural driver is behind-the-meter power generation, which Baker claims can multiply a small town's tax revenues by roughly 10x, while dismissing water consumption concerns as debunked. He further notes that US natural gas at $2–3/MMBtu versus $20–25/MMBtu in Europe and Asia creates a durable manufacturing and energy cost advantage that underpins the US re-industrialization thesis. The investment implication is a structural long on US data center infrastructure, power generation, and the trades/construction ecosystem, though Baker does not name specific equity beneficiaries in this segment.

summary: Jalapeno (Meta's internal ASIC) is the first genuinely competitive internal ASIC outside of TPU and Trainium, but it only competes with one of Nvidia's nine chips
summary_extended: Baker argues that Meta's internally developed ASIC, codenamed Jalapeno, represents a meaningful milestone as the first genuinely competitive internal chip he has seen outside of Google's TPU and Amazon's Trainium, achieved in a remarkably short development timeframe. He attributes this success to a structural advantage that vertically integrated labs possess: because they own the model and can see the direction of research, they have an inherent edge in designing chips optimized for their own workloads. However, Baker immediately contextualizes the achievement by noting that competing with Nvidia at the full system level requires not just one chip but nine distinct chips working together, and Jalapeno only addresses one of those nine. The investment implication is nuanced: while Meta's chip progress is real and could reduce its dependence on Nvidia over time, the scope of Nvidia's system-level moat remains vast, and Jalapeno does not represent an imminent threat to Nvidia's dominance across the full datacenter stack. Baker's framing suggests Nvidia's competitive position is more durable than a single-chip comparison would imply, making this a moderately bullish signal for Nvidia's medium-term moat and a cautiously positive data point for Meta's long-term capex efficiency.
